newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German talks yield few surprises - economists.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German talks yield few surprises - economists.

text.p: Talks between top French and German finance officials on Wednesday appeared to contain little to surprise financial markets, economists said.

"To me it sounded like the confidence-inspiring statements we were expecting," BIP-Dresdner economist Marie Owens-Thomsen said after the talks between the French and German finance ministers and central bank heads.

The ministers reaffirmed their commitment to press ahead with European monetary union on time on January 1, 1999, and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the question of delaying the single currency had "most definitely not" played a part in discussions in the central French city of Lyon.

There has been some speculation in financial markets that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) might be delayed because of Germany's difficulties in reducing its budget deficit this year to three percent of gross domestic product in line with Maastricht treaty requirements.

"They said more or less what was expected by the market. They're quite confident about Maastrict and the realisation of three percent (budget deficit to GDP ratio)," Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said.
"They're quite optimistic about growth, and there maybe they're not wrong" although hitting the three percent target is less of a certaintly, he said.
"The stability council was also more or less as expected. That it would be an informal body was clear," he added.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel reiterated support for an informal stability council to oversee economic policies after the launch of the single currency.

"In all honesty there was not really a great deal that surprised me. The stability council was one of the things people focused on but from what I've seen of the agreements it's questionable whether it will have any meaningful role," David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London, said.
"They've agreed to it, but I think the Germans see it more as a talking shop, rather than anything to seriously impede the central bank's work," he added.
"Nothing stands out. The market expected them to get together and slap each others backs and stress their commitment to Maastricht. They're not exactly going to say anything different," he said.

He said he was confident France would meet its target of reducing its budget deficit to three percent of GDP this year from an estimated 4.1 percent last year, while Germany's success in this would depend on political will.

"Yes, the French will hit three percent. Looking at the history of French budgets their record of getting within 0.1 of their targets is excellent. The bottom line comes down to how much the German government is determined to do it, it's not a question of can they do it, but will they do it?"

He also said that one of the more interesting developments in recent days was a shift in the position of the Bundesbank, whose members are now stressing the need for EMU to go ahead on time rather than the importance of a strict interpretation of Maastricht treaty criteria.
"The Bundesbank has clearly shifted its position," he said.
